model.name: Person
model.purpose: Describe the natural person as a civil identity and life-course legal subject: the registered identity, its documents and scheme-qualified identifiers, civil status, legal capacity and representation, and the person-controlled contact and self-declared sphere to which other models attach.
model.scope_statement: This model covers one living or deceased natural person as a civil-identity subject. It holds the identity core (who the person is before the law), evidence of that identity, life-course legal states, and the personal-sphere attributes the person controls. It does not model the biological organism, fictional or legal persons, household or filiation graphs, organisational roles, health records, or full address/location geometries. Documents and identifiers evidence identity; they do not constitute the person.
in_scope: The natural person as a registered legal identity that may be living or deceased but not imaginary

Legal identity characteristics conferred by civil registration or a legally recognised identification authority: name, recorded sex or gender marker, place and date of birth, and retirement by death registration
Structured, versioned names with script, ordering convention and validity
Issued identity documents and credentials that evidence identity, including travel documents and national identity cards
Scheme-qualified identifiers assigned by named authorities, including eIDAS person identification data
Registered civil status as a legal state of the person, distinct from household membership
Legal capacity, age-based minority, emancipation, supported decision-making and remaining national guardianship or representation arrangements
Citizenship, statelessness and refugee proof-of-identity as legal ties to jurisdictions
Person-controlled contact points and pointers to domicile and residency
Self-declared alternative names, preferences and similar attributes under the person's control
Data-subject rights, consent grants, verification without over-disclosure, record quality, correction, retention and public or statistical extracts
out_of_scope: The person as a biological organism, clinical patient, genome, biometric template store or health record (including HL7 FHIR Patient)
Legal persons, organisations, devices, services, agents that are not natural persons, and fictional, mythical or undead characters
Household, family, filiation, parent, child, spouse-as-relationship, kinship and membership graphs, which belong in a household or family sibling model
Population groups, communities, cohorts and statistical units as group entities
Education, qualifications, occupations, employment, roles in organisations and programme membership
Full address, cadastral, geospatial and location master data beyond a pointer or reuse of an address value shape
Travel, visa, border-control operational processes beyond the identity document as evidence
Consent, access-control and audit ledgers as standalone governance models, which are referenced rather than copied
Religion, ethnicity, political opinion, health, sex life and other special-category profiles except where a civil marker is legally recorded
Assets, property, contracts, beneficial ownership and politically exposed person roles

boundary_notes.neighbor: UN Legal Identity Agenda civil registration
boundary_notes.distinction: UN operational legal identity is created by birth registration (or by a legally recognised identification authority linked to civil registration) and retired by death registration; the historical register remains.
SEMIC Core Person Vocabulary treats Person as a non-imaginary individual and a subclass of Agent, and explicitly excludes roles and relationships from the person core.

boundary_notes.neighbor: ICAO Doc 9303 machine readable travel documents
boundary_notes.distinction: ICAO Doc 9303 specifies travel-document evidence, not the civil identity itself.
ISO/IEC 24760-1 supplies identity, identifier and identity-proofing vocabulary for any information system, including non-human principals, and is therefore an alignment, not a person schema.

boundary_notes.neighbor: OASIS CIQ name and address specifications
boundary_notes.distinction: OASIS CIQ supplies reusable name and address value shapes.
GDPR defines the natural person as data subject and does not apply to legal persons.
Household membership, filiation and spouse-as-relationship resolve in a sibling model that points here.
CPV records sex as the organism's biological sex; this model stores only the legally recorded marker and leaves organism traits to a biology or health model.

boundary_notes.neighbor: National civil-status, capacity and name-part code lists
boundary_notes.distinction: No single global civil-status, capacity or name-part code list is claimed.

bundles.name: Civil identity
bundles.description: The registered natural-person identity as a legal subject, the versioned name facts that name it, the documents that evidence it, and the scheme-qualified identifiers that refer to it without becoming it.
bundles.rationale: Keeps the registrar-owned identity core separate from the names, documents and identifiers that evidence or refer to it, so that evidence never becomes the subject.

layers.name: Identity core
layers.description: Who the natural person is before the law: canonical identity, vital status, birth and death facts, and the legally recorded sex or gender marker.

findings.name: Registered natural person
findings.description: A Person in this model is one individual human being who may be dead or alive but not imaginary, recognised as a person before the law. Legal identity is the basic characteristics of that individual — at least name, sex, place and date of birth — conferred through registration and a certificate by an authorised civil registration authority after birth, or, if birth was not registered, by a legally recognised identification authority that must be linked to civil registration. The person is the stable subject; identifiers, documents and names attach to the person. ISO/IEC 24760 identity vocabulary applies, but that standard also covers non-human principals and is not itself a natural-person schema. Schema.org Person additionally allows fictional and undead characters and is therefore only a public-projection alignment.

questions.text: What authoritative master-system identifier does the civil registrar or legally recognised identification authority treat as the canonical identity of this natural person?
answer_data: assigned-at (RFC 3339 datetime with seconds and offset)
dimension-uuid-or-ulid (only if no master identifier exists)

questions.text: Is this identity currently living, deceased, or in an unresolved legal status such as missing or presumed dead, and which register entry supports that status?
Does this record represent a natural person rather than a legal person, device, fictional character or biological specimen, and which rule excludes the other kinds?

data_elements.name: Canonical person identifier
data_elements.description: Authoritative master-system identifier from the civil register or identification authority; fallback governed IRI; else UUID or ULID assigned by the adopting Dimension. A date is not an identifier.

data_elements.name: Vital status
data_elements.description: Living, deceased, missing, presumed-dead or unknown, with effective time separate from observation time.

data_elements.name: Registration or identification authority
data_elements.description: Organisation identifier of the civil registrar or legally recognised identification authority that confers legal identity.

data_elements.name: Governed global IRI
data_elements.description: Stable IRI for the person when a global identifier is published under a governed namespace.

artifacts.name: Civil register person record
artifacts.description: Master legal-identity record maintained by the civil registration or identification authority for one natural person.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Identified by the master person identifier assigned by the civil registration or identification authority.

findings.name: Birth and death facts
findings.description: Date and place of birth, and where applicable date and place of death, are core legal-identity characteristics. CPV allows incomplete dates via GenericDate (xs:date, gYearMonth or gYear) because birth and death dates are often only partially known. Event time of birth or death is distinct from the time the fact was registered or ingested. Country coding should prefer ISO 3166-1, noting the EU Publications Office exceptions EL for Greece and UK for the United Kingdom versus ISO GR and GB.

questions.text: What is the person's date of birth, at what precision is it known, and is that the event time or the registration time?
answer_data: birth-event-date (GenericDate: full date, year-month or year)

questions.text: Where was the person born, using which geographic identifier and which country code list?
answer_data: historic-country-iso-3166-3 (if the country no longer exists)

questions.text: If the person is deceased, what are the date and place of death, and do they come from a death certificate rather than an informal report?

data_elements.name: Date of birth
data_elements.description: GenericDate for the birth event; not an identifier. Store event time and registration/observation time separately.

data_elements.name: Place of birth
data_elements.description: Location name plus preferred geographic IRI and country code.

data_elements.name: Date of death
data_elements.description: GenericDate for the death event when registered; empty while living.

data_elements.name: Country code system
data_elements.description: Which country list is in use, including ISO 3166-1 versus OP/EU EL and UK exceptions.

artifacts.name: Birth certificate
artifacts.description: Legal instrument issued by the civil registration authority that evidences birth facts and confers legal identity.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Issuer-assigned certificate number qualified by the issuing civil registration authority and register entry.

artifacts.name: Death certificate
artifacts.description: Legal instrument that registers death and retires legal identity without deleting the historical record.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Issuer-assigned certificate number qualified by the issuing civil registration authority and register entry.

findings.name: Sex, gender and document markers
findings.description: UN legal identity lists sex among the basic characteristics conferred at registration. CPV 2.1.2 splits gender (identities, expressions and societal roles, with an explicitly stated controlled vocabulary) from sex (the organism's biological sex, recommended Publications Office human-sex table). ICAO Doc 9303 records holder sex on travel documents as F, M or X/unspecified. Those three systems are not equivalent: the civil register stores a legally recorded marker and its vocabulary, not a biological organism model. Marker changes are civil events with authority and effective time.

questions.text: Which legally recorded sex or gender marker is currently on the civil identity, under which controlled vocabulary, and who recorded it?
What sex value is printed or encoded on each current identity document, and does it differ from the civil register marker?
Has the legally recorded marker changed, under what legal basis, and over which effective period?

data_elements.name: Civil sex or gender marker
data_elements.description: Coded marker as recorded by the registrar, always paired with an explicit vocabulary IRI.

data_elements.name: ICAO document sex
data_elements.description: Travel-document sex field M, F or X/unspecified, which may diverge from the civil marker.

data_elements.name: Marker vocabulary
data_elements.description: Controlled vocabulary actually used (civil, CPV gender, Publications Office sex, ICAO).

artifacts.name: Marker recording or change decision
artifacts.description: Registrar or court instrument that records or changes the legally held sex or gender marker.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Identified by the deciding registrar or court instrument identifier together with its effective period.

layers.name: Legal name
layers.description: Versioned, structured names that name the person without being the person, including cultural name-part semantics.

findings.name: Structured legal name
findings.description: CPV provides full name, given name, family name, patronymic, matronymic, birth name and alternative name, and allows more than one full legal name. Names persist independently of address and are insufficient alone to identify a person. OASIS xNL separates structure from semantics so that FirstName/MiddleName/LastName are not forced on cultures that do not use them; PersonNameElement types are a customisable code list (for example Russian Name/FathersName/FamilyName). eIDAS person identification data mandates current family name and current given names, including middle names where applicable. ICAO splits primary and secondary identifiers and requires Latin MRZ transliteration. A name has script, language, ordering convention and a validity period.

questions.text: What is the current legal name, in which parts, script, language and ordering convention, and which full-name string is the canonical rendering?
Over which period is this name legally effective, and which instrument made it effective?
What is the birth name, and which alternative or professional names are recorded without being legal names?
answer_data: alternative-names[] (text, language, usage: professional | commonly-known | other)

data_elements.name: Person name record
data_elements.description: One versioned name with parts, script, language, ordering and validity.

data_elements.name: Name-part scheme
data_elements.description: Which semantic list is used for name elements, because Anglo-American first/middle/last is not universal.

data_elements.name: MRZ transliterated name
data_elements.description: ICAO Latin primary and secondary identifiers used on travel documents.

artifacts.name: Name registration entry
artifacts.description: Register entry or deed that establishes a legal name version, including name-change instruments.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Identified by the register entry or instrument identifier that establishes the name version, with its validity period.

layers.name: Identity document
layers.description: Issued documents and credentials that evidence identity and never constitute it.

findings.name: Issued identity document
findings.description: Proof of legal identity is a credential such as a birth certificate, identity card or digital identity credential recognised under national law. ICAO Doc 9303 specifies MRTD data: issuing state, document type and number, primary and secondary name identifiers, nationality, date of birth, sex, optional place of birth, personal number, dates of issue and expiry, issuing authority, portrait, and for eMRTDs data groups including DG1 biographical data and DG2 face (optional fingerprints and iris). EU identity cards must meet ICAO 9303 ID-1/MRZ rules. eIDAS electronic identification means contain person identification data uniquely representing the natural person. Documents can be revoked before expiry. Biometric images on a chip evidence the holder of the document; they are not a licence to copy an organism or health model.

questions.text: What document uniquely evidences this person, of which type, issued by whom, and under which document number in which scheme?
answer_data: document-type-code (passport | identity-card | residence-document | birth-certificate | digital-pid | other)

questions.text: Is the document valid, expired, revoked or suspended, and what are the issue, expiry and revocation times?
How is the document bound to this person rather than to another person with a similar name?

data_elements.name: Document number
data_elements.description: Issuer-assigned number that identifies the document instance, not the person.

data_elements.name: Document lifecycle state
data_elements.description: Valid, expired, revoked, suspended or cancelled.

data_elements.name: Issuing authority
data_elements.description: State or organisation that issued the document, distinct from the civil registrar when they differ.

data_elements.name: Machine-readable zone data
data_elements.description: ICAO MRZ fields used for inspection and as DG1 content.

artifacts.name: Machine-readable travel or identity document
artifacts.description: Passport, identity card or other MRTD/eMRTD issued under ICAO Doc 9303 or equivalent national identity-card rules.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Issuer-assigned document number qualified by issuing state, document type and number scheme.

artifacts.name: Person identification data credential
artifacts.description: eIDAS electronic identification means or EUDI Wallet PID that uniquely represents the natural person.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Issuer-assigned credential identifier together with the PID unique person identifier it carries.

layers.name: Identifier scheme
layers.description: Identifiers assigned under named schemes; an identifier refers to the person and is not the person.

findings.name: Scheme-qualified identifiers
findings.description: CPV Identifier (ADMS/UN CEFACT) carries notation, issuing authority, date of issue, scheme agency and the person identified. ISO/IEC 24760 distinguishes identity, attribute, identifier and principal: many identifiers may attach to one identity. eIDAS requires a person identifier in the minimum data set; that unique identifier is nationality-code structured and may be pairwise or derived, so it must not be assumed to equal a national personal number. Dates are not identifiers.

questions.text: Which identifiers are currently assigned to this person, under which schemes, by which authorities, and with which validity?
answer_data: identifier-assignment[]: scheme-iri, scheme-name, notation, issuing-authority-id, issued-at (RFC 3339), valid-from, valid-to, status (active | retired | replaced)

questions.text: What eIDAS or PID person identifier is in use, is it pairwise to a destination country, and may it be used for record matching?
Which identifier, if any, is treated as canonical, and what rule prevents treating any identifier as the person?

data_elements.name: Identifier assignment
data_elements.description: One scheme, notation, issuer and validity bound to the person.

data_elements.name: Identifier scheme
data_elements.description: URI or name of the scheme used to construct the identifier.

data_elements.name: eIDAS person identifier
data_elements.description: Minimum-data-set unique identifier, which may be derived or pairwise.

artifacts.name: Identifier assignment register extract
artifacts.description: Authority record of an identifier assigned under a named scheme.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Identified by the assignment record identifier held by the assigning authority, qualified by scheme IRI.

bundles.name: Life course
bundles.description: The person through time as a legal subject: creation and retirement of legal identity, civil status, legal capacity and representation, and citizenship or statelessness.
bundles.rationale: Groups the legal states that open, change and retire the person as a legal subject, so that history is carried by registered events rather than by mutable attributes.

layers.name: Vital registration
layers.description: Birth registration creates legal identity; death registration retires it; exceptional paths exist when birth was not registered.

findings.name: Identity creation and retirement
findings.description: Civil registration is the continuous, permanent, compulsory and universal recording of vital events. Legal identity is conferred by birth registration and a certificate, or by a legally recognised identification authority linked to civil registration. Legal identity is retired by issuance of a death certificate. UNFPA states that universal death registration ends legal identity and status. The register itself is permanent: retirement is not deletion. CRC Article 7 and ICCPR Article 24(2), as cited by UN LIA, require birth registration and a name. SDG 16.9 is legal identity for all, including birth registration.

questions.text: When and where was birth registered, by which registrar, and was legal identity conferred at registration or later by an identification authority?
When was death registered, which certificate retired legal identity, and is the person record closed or still updateable for historical correction?
If birth was not registered immediately, which identification authority conferred legal identity, and is that authority linked to the civil register?

data_elements.name: Birth registration identifier
data_elements.description: Register identifier of the birth event that created or should have created legal identity.

data_elements.name: Death registration identifier
data_elements.description: Register identifier of the death event that retires legal identity.

data_elements.name: Identity conferral path
data_elements.description: Civil registration versus later identification-authority conferral linked to CRVS.

artifacts.name: Vital event register entry
artifacts.description: Permanent civil-registration entry for birth or death, including late registration.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Register entry identifier assigned by the registrar, qualified by register, jurisdiction and event type.

findings.name: Exceptional identity paths
findings.description: UN LIA explicitly covers persons whose birth was not registered and refugees whose proof of legal identity may be issued by the host State or an internationally mandated authority. Statelessness is a named UN LIA concern. National CRVS practice also includes foundlings, unknown parentage, incomplete dates, delayed registration and, in some jurisdictions, presumed death and later identity restoration. Those last national cases are recorded here as operating needs with incomplete global normative detail.

questions.text: Is proof of legal identity issued by a host State or by an internationally mandated authority for a refugee or similar status, and how does it link to this person?
Was this identity opened for a foundling or person of unknown parentage, and which placeholder name and birth facts were assigned?
Has legal identity been retired by presumed death or later restored, and what is the current vital status?

data_elements.name: Proof of identity issuer kind
data_elements.description: Host State versus internationally mandated authority for refugees.

data_elements.name: Foundling or unknown parentage flag
data_elements.description: Marks identities opened without ordinary parental birth facts.

data_elements.name: Presumed-death order
data_elements.description: National court or registrar instrument; global UN LIA text does not specify this path.

artifacts.name: Refugee or mandated identity credential
artifacts.description: Proof of legal identity issued by a State or internationally mandated authority.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Issuer-assigned credential number qualified by the host State or internationally mandated authority that issued it.

layers.name: Civil status
layers.description: The registered civil state of the person as a legal subject, not the household graph of partners and relatives.

findings.name: Registered civil status
findings.description: UN CRVS treats marriage, divorce and related vital events as registered facts that establish civil status and family situation. Civil status is a current legal state of the person (for example never-married, married, registered partnership, divorced, widowed, legally separated) with effective date and registering authority. The partner, household and filiation links belong in a household or family sibling model that points here. Status history is carried by events; there is one current status per jurisdiction unless national law allows concurrent statuses.

questions.text: What is the person's current registered civil status in each relevant jurisdiction, from when, and according to which register?
Which vital event last changed civil status, and what are the event and registration times?
answer_data: event-type (marriage | divorce | annulment | partnership-registration | partnership-dissolution | widowhood | legal-separation | other)

questions.text: Does any recorded partner or household membership live in this person record, or is it only a pointer to a household or family model?

data_elements.name: Civil status code
data_elements.description: Current registered civil state in a named jurisdiction; no single global code list is claimed.

data_elements.name: Civil status effective time
data_elements.description: RFC 3339 effective time of the current status.

data_elements.name: Civil status event type
data_elements.description: Vital event that changed status, stored as an event reference rather than a household edge.

artifacts.name: Civil status certificate
artifacts.description: Marriage, divorce, partnership or equivalent certificate evidencing a civil-status event, used here only as status evidence.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Issuer-assigned certificate number qualified by the registering authority and jurisdiction.

layers.name: Legal capacity and representation
layers.description: Capacity to hold rights and to act, support in exercising capacity, and remaining national representation arrangements.

findings.name: Capacity and representation
findings.description: ICCPR Article 16 and CRPD Article 12 affirm recognition as a person before the law. CRPD Article 12 requires legal capacity on an equal basis in all aspects of life, access to support in exercising that capacity, and safeguards that respect will and preferences, avoid conflict of interest, are proportional, time-limited and independently reviewed. GDPR Article 8 sets conditions for a child's consent in information-society services, so minority remains an operating fact even where legal capacity is universal. Many States still operate substitute decision-making (guardianship, tutelle, conservatorship, emancipation). The CRPD Committee reads Article 12 as requiring a shift from substitute to supported decision-making; that reading is an interpretive conflict with much national law and is recorded, not resolved. Representation of a natural person by another natural person is also an eIDAS identification case.

questions.text: What legal-capacity class applies now, on what basis, for which acts, and over which period?
answer_data: capacity-class (full | minority | emancipated | supported | restricted-national | unknown)

questions.text: Who may support or represent this person, under which model, for which scope, and with which safeguards and review date?
answer_data: arrangement-kind (supported-decision-making | power-of-attorney | guardianship | parental-responsibility | eidas-representation | other)

questions.text: What is the person's age-of-majority jurisdiction rule, and who may consent to processing while the person is a child?

data_elements.name: Capacity class
data_elements.description: Current legal-capacity classification, always with basis, scope and period.

data_elements.name: Representation or support arrangement
data_elements.description: Supported decision-making, parental responsibility, power of attorney, guardianship or eIDAS representation.

data_elements.name: Age of majority rule
data_elements.description: Jurisdiction-specific majority age used to compute minority, not a global constant.

artifacts.name: Capacity, support or guardianship instrument
artifacts.description: Court order, support agreement, emancipation instrument or parental-responsibility record.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Identified by the issuing court or authority instrument identifier, with recorded scope and review date.

layers.name: Citizenship and nationality
layers.description: Legal ties to jurisdictions, including none (statelessness) and multiple citizenships.

findings.name: Citizenship ties
findings.description: CPV models citizenship as a relationship to a Jurisdiction that conferred citizenship rights, and states that a person may have one, several or no citizenships. CPV treats citizenship as a legal status distinct from the more cultural term nationality. ICAO travel documents nevertheless encode nationality. UN LIA highlights statelessness and refugee proof of identity. Residency and domicile are not citizenship.

questions.text: Which jurisdictions have conferred citizenship on this person, from when, and is the person stateless?
answer_data: citizenship[]: jurisdiction-id, status (citizen | national | stateless | disputed | unknown), conferred-at (RFC 3339), basis (birth | descent | naturalisation | other), evidence-document-id

questions.text: What nationality is encoded on current travel documents, and does it differ from registered citizenships?
If the person is stateless or a refugee, which authority recognises that status and which credential proves legal identity?

data_elements.name: Citizenship tie
data_elements.description: Relationship to a jurisdiction that conferred citizenship, with time and basis.

data_elements.name: Statelessness flag
data_elements.description: True when no citizenship is held or when statelessness is recognised.

data_elements.name: Document nationality
data_elements.description: Nationality as encoded on an ICAO travel document.

artifacts.name: Citizenship, naturalisation or protection instrument
artifacts.description: Naturalisation certificate, citizenship register extract, or recognised stateless/refugee identity proof.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Issuer-assigned instrument number qualified by the conferring or recognising authority and jurisdiction.

bundles.name: Personal sphere
bundles.description: Attributes and channels the person declares and controls, distinct from registrar-owned civil facts.
bundles.rationale: Separates person-owned declarations, channels and rights from registrar-owned civil facts, so that ownership and no-silent-overwrite rules stay explicit.

layers.name: Contact and presence
layers.description: Person-controlled contact points and pointers to domicile and residency, without owning the address master.

findings.name: Contact, domicile and residency
findings.description: CPV 2.1.2 adds Contact Point (email, telephone, contact page) on Person. Domicile is the place treated as permanent home, typed as Address. Residency is a Jurisdiction where the person has their dwelling; CPV notes a person may have one, several or no residency statuses. Those two properties overlap in wording with classical domicile versus habitual residence and must be stored with explicit legal sense. Full address structure is reused from Core Location or OASIS xAL by reference or embed of a value shape, not as a competing location master. Contact values are personal data under GDPR.

questions.text: Which contact channels does the person currently declare, of which type, with which visibility, and who may use them?
answer_data: contact-point[]: channel-type (email | telephone | contact-page | other), value-pointer-or-handle, valid-from, valid-to, visibility (private | restricted | public), intended-use

questions.text: What is the current domicile (permanent home) pointer, in which legal sense, and which address record does it reference?
In which jurisdictions does the person have residency or habitual residence, and is any of those distinct from domicile?
answer_data: residency[]: jurisdiction-id, status (resident | habitual-resident | none), valid-from, valid-to, distinct-from-domicile (boolean)

data_elements.name: Contact point
data_elements.description: Person-controlled channel with type, value pointer, validity and visibility.

data_elements.name: Domicile pointer
data_elements.description: Reference to an address record for the place treated as permanent home.

data_elements.name: Residency jurisdiction
data_elements.description: Jurisdiction of dwelling or habitual residence, which may be multiple or none.

artifacts.name: Contact and abode declaration
artifacts.description: Person- or registrar-sourced declaration of contact channels, domicile pointer and residency.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Identified by the declaration record identifier together with the declaring party (person, registrar or court).

layers.name: Self-declared attributes
layers.description: Non-legal names, preferences and similar facts under the person's control.

findings.name: Self-declared personal attributes
findings.description: CPV alternative name records names by which a person is generally or professionally known that are not legal names, and excludes pet names of no consequence in public-sector exchange. Schema.org additionally publishes pronouns and gender as typically person-authoritative expression; those are useful for self-view and public projection but are not civil-register facts. This layer is owned by the person as data subject. It must not overwrite registrar-owned legal name, sex marker or civil status.

questions.text: What name does the person currently prefer for non-legal use, and in which contexts may it be shown?
What gender expression or pronouns, if any, does the person declare for self-view or public projection, and which vocabulary is used?
Which of these attributes may the registrar never treat as legal name or civil marker without a separate civil event?

data_elements.name: Preferred non-legal name
data_elements.description: Self-declared name for contexts that do not require the legal name.

data_elements.name: Self-declared pronouns
data_elements.description: Optional expression data for self-view or public projection, never a civil-register substitute.

data_elements.name: Visibility setting
data_elements.description: Person-controlled disclosure level for each self-declared attribute.

artifacts.name: Self-declaration record
artifacts.description: Person-authored record of preferred name, pronouns or similar attributes with visibility.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Identified by the self-declaration record identifier owned by the person, with declaration time.

layers.name: Subject rights and consent
layers.description: The person as GDPR data subject: lawful basis, consent, access, rectification, erasure, restriction and portability, constrained by permanent civil registration.

findings.name: Data-subject rights and grants
findings.description: GDPR applies to identified or identifiable natural persons regardless of nationality or residence, not to legal persons. Personal data include name, identification number, location data, online identifiers and factors of physical, physiological, genetic, mental, economic, cultural or social identity. Consent must be freely given, specific, informed, unambiguous and withdrawable. Biometric data for unique identification are a special category. Rights include access, rectification, erasure, restriction, portability and objection. Storage limitation has a public-interest archiving, research and statistics exception that is the usual basis for permanent civil registers. Erasure of registrar-owned vital records therefore conflicts with UN permanence unless a national law provides a narrow path. Detailed consent ledgers belong in a sibling consent model.

questions.text: For each processing of this person's data, what is the lawful basis, and if consent, can it be demonstrated and withdrawn?
answer_data: lawful-basis (consent | contract | legal-obligation | vital-interests | public-task | legitimate-interests)

questions.text: Which attributes are subject to erasure or restriction on request, and which are retained as permanent civil-registration archives?
What self-view or portable extract is the person entitled to, and what was last disclosed to them?

data_elements.name: Lawful basis
data_elements.description: GDPR Article 6 basis for a stated purpose, with consent identifier when applicable.

data_elements.name: Retention regime
data_elements.description: Whether an attribute is personal-sphere erasable, restrictable, or a permanent civil-register fact.

data_elements.name: Consent grant identifier
data_elements.description: Pointer to a consent record in the sibling consent model.

artifacts.name: Data-subject rights request and decision
artifacts.description: Access, rectification, erasure, restriction or portability request and the controller decision.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Identified by the request identifier assigned by the controller, bound to the person and the decision time.

bundles.name: Assurance and governance
bundles.description: How identity is proved and matched, how records are quality-managed, and how attributes are disclosed, retained or withheld.
bundles.rationale: Collects the proofing, quality and disclosure rules that determine how much of the person may be asserted, corrected or released, so that verification never becomes bulk disclosure.

layers.name: Verification and matching
layers.description: Identity proofing and verification that confirm attributes without unnecessary disclosure.

findings.name: Identity proofing and verification
findings.description: ISO/IEC 24760-1 defines identity-proofing among core identity-management terms for any system that processes identity information. eIDAS electronic identification uses person identification data uniquely representing the natural person, with assurance levels, selective disclosure in the European Digital Identity Wallet, and a minimum data set of current family name, current first names, date of birth and person identifier. Record matching must not assume that an eIDAS unique identifier equals a national personal number. Verification answers should confirm only what was asked.

questions.text: At what assurance or proofing level was this person identified, by which scheme, and when?
Which attributes were requested for a verification, which were confirmed, and which were withheld?
Which keys are authorised for matching this person to another record, and which identifiers are pairwise and therefore unusable for match?

data_elements.name: Identity assurance level
data_elements.description: eIDAS or other scheme assurance/proofing level attached to an identification event.

data_elements.name: Verification response
data_elements.description: Confirmation-only or selectively disclosed attributes for one request.

data_elements.name: Record-matching key
data_elements.description: Authorised persistent identifier or attribute set; excludes pairwise eIDAS UIDs where policy forbids.

artifacts.name: Identity verification result
artifacts.description: Proofing or authentication result stating assurance level and attributes confirmed without exporting unused personal data.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Identified by the verification request identifier together with the proofing authority and answer time.

layers.name: Quality and correction
layers.description: Accuracy, completeness, late registration, duplicate detection and rectification.

findings.name: Record quality and correction
findings.description: UN civil registration is intended to be complete, continuous and accurate. OASIS CIQ treats unstructured name data as poor quality and provides data-quality metadata. GDPR requires accuracy and rectification without delay. CPV notes that all individual data may change and that birth names tend to persist. Duplicate person records, delayed registration and incomplete dates are operating facts. Provenance must record who asserted a fact, from which evidence, and when it was observed versus when the event occurred.

questions.text: Who asserted each identity fact, from which evidence, at which event time and which observation time?
Which mandatory legal-identity characteristics are missing or only partial, and is this record a suspected duplicate of another person?
Which corrections have been applied, under which legal basis, and do they supersede prior versions without rewriting history?

data_elements.name: Fact provenance
data_elements.description: Asserter, evidence, event time and observation/ingestion time for one fact.

data_elements.name: Completeness flags
data_elements.description: Which UN legal-identity characteristics are absent or partial.

data_elements.name: Duplicate candidate
data_elements.description: Possible other person record and investigation status.

artifacts.name: Correction or rectification entry
artifacts.description: Versioned correction that preserves prior values and legal basis.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Identified by the correction identifier together with the corrected fact identifier and the superseded record identifier.

layers.name: Disclosure and retention
layers.description: Who may see which projection of the person, for how long, and which extracts leave the register.

findings.name: Projections, retention and extracts
findings.description: Different projections are required: a verification view that omits unasked attributes; a public-record extract limited to what registration law makes public; a self-view of records and grants; and anonymised vital-statistics aggregates for the statistics office. eIDAS wallets require selective disclosure under user control. GDPR storage limitation coexists with UN permanence of civil registration via the archiving exception. Access exceptions include child representation, court orders, and legally mandated statistical or law-enforcement extracts.

questions.text: For a named requester and purpose, which projection may be produced and which attributes must be omitted?
What is the retention, archive or deletion rule for each attribute class, and when would deletion actually occur?
Which exception, if any, allows access without the person's current consent, and what audit evidence is required?

data_elements.name: Projection type
data_elements.description: verified-identity, public-record, self-view, vital-statistics or pid-selective.

data_elements.name: Retention rule
data_elements.description: Per-attribute-class permanence, archive or deletion rule.

data_elements.name: Access exception type
data_elements.description: Lawful exception to default person-or-registrar access control.

artifacts.name: Public record or vital-statistics extract
artifacts.description: Lawful extract that omits the personal sphere or anonymises identity for statistics.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Identified by the extract identifier together with the purpose and legal basis under which it was released.

artifacts.name: Self-view export
artifacts.description: Portable or inspectable package of records and grants concerning the person.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Identified by the portable extract identifier bound to the person and the disclosure time.

functions.name: Register birth
functions.description: Create a natural-person legal identity by recording a birth vital event and issuing a birth certificate, or record a late registration linked to an identification-authority conferral.
inputs: Birth event facts including name, recorded sex marker, and place and date of birth
Conferral path indicator for ordinary or late registration
outputs: Person record with conferred legal identity
preconditions: The registering body is an authorised civil registration authority, or a legally recognised identification authority linked to civil registration
effects: Legal identity is conferred on the natural person
A permanent vital-event register entry exists for the birth

functions.name: Register death
functions.description: Retire legal identity by recording a death vital event and issuing a death certificate, without deleting the permanent historical register.
inputs: Death event facts including date and place of death
preconditions: A registered person record exists whose legal identity has not already been retired by a registered death
effects: Legal identity is retired
The permanent historical register entry is preserved rather than deleted

functions.name: Assign identifier
functions.description: Attach a scheme-qualified identifier to the person with issuer, notation, issue time and validity, without treating the identifier as the identity.
outputs: Identifier assignment attached to the person with status active, retired or replaced
preconditions: The scheme and its issuing authority are named
effects: The person can be referred to under the named scheme
The identifier refers to the person and does not become the person

functions.name: Issue identity document
functions.description: Issue a proof of legal identity such as an identity card, passport or digital PID bound to the person, including ICAO or eIDAS mandatory fields.
outputs: Issued identity document or PID credential with document number, validity dates and holder binding
preconditions: Legal identity has been conferred on the person
The issuer is an authorised document issuer
effects: A proof of legal identity bound to the person exists
Document lifecycle state is set to valid

functions.name: Revoke identity document
functions.description: Invalidate a document before expiry and record revocation time, authority and reason.
outputs: Document state set to revoked with revocation time, authority and reason
preconditions: The document exists and has not already expired or been cancelled
effects: The document is no longer valid evidence of identity
The revoked document remains historically recorded in a revoked state

functions.name: Change legal name
functions.description: Take a new legal name version into effect with validity period, instrument and registrar, preserving prior name history.
inputs: New name parts with script, language tag and ordering convention
outputs: New effective-dated legal name version with validity period
preconditions: An instrument or registered event supports the new legal name
effects: The prior name version is closed with a validity end and preserved as history
Self-declared names are not promoted to legal names by this function

functions.name: Change civil status
functions.description: Update the person's current civil status from a registered vital event while leaving household membership to a sibling model.
outputs: Updated current civil status with effective time, registering authority and register entry
preconditions: The change derives from a registered vital event such as marriage, divorce, annulment, partnership registration or dissolution
effects: The prior civil status is superseded and retained as history
Partner, household and filiation links remain in the sibling model

functions.name: Establish support or representation
functions.description: Record a supported-decision-making, parental-responsibility, power-of-attorney, guardianship or eIDAS representation arrangement with scope, safeguards and review date.
inputs: Safeguards, will-and-preferences record and review date
outputs: Recorded representation or support arrangement with scope, safeguards and review due date
preconditions: A competent court, statute, or the person where the law allows, establishes the arrangement
effects: Named parties may act within the recorded scope
The arrangement is proportional, time-limited and subject to independent review

functions.name: Verify identity
functions.description: Answer an identity-proofing or authentication request at a stated assurance level, confirming only requested attributes.
inputs: Verification request with requested attribute identifiers
outputs: Verification result stating assurance level and confirmed attributes, with withheld attributes recorded
preconditions: The requester states a purpose and a lawful basis for the verification
effects: Only requested attributes are confirmed or selectively disclosed
The verification leaves an audit trail

functions.name: Match person records
functions.description: Decide whether two records refer to the same natural person using authorised persistent keys, not pairwise eIDAS identifiers where those cannot be reused.
outputs: Match decision with match confidence and investigation status
preconditions: Only authorised persistent keys are used, and pairwise eIDAS identifiers are excluded where they may not be reused for matching
effects: Suspected duplicates are flagged with confidence and investigation status
An eIDAS person identifier is not treated as a national personal number

functions.name: Exercise data-subject rights
functions.description: Process access, rectification, erasure, restriction or portability requests, applying permanent-register overrides where civil-registration law requires retention.
inputs: Data-subject request of type access, rectification, erasure, restriction or portability
outputs: Per-attribute decision with retention regime and decision time
Portable or self-view extract where the right applies
preconditions: The requester is the person or an authorised representative
effects: Personal-sphere attributes may be erased or restricted
Permanent civil-register facts are retained under the public-interest archiving override
The decision is audited

functions.name: Produce vital-statistics extract
functions.description: Release anonymised aggregates of registrations to the statistics office without exporting the personal sphere.
inputs: Registration events for the reporting period
preconditions: The statistical use is legally mandated
effects: Aggregates are released without exporting the personal sphere
Recipients must not re-identify persons from the aggregates

composition.purpose: Align classes and properties with SEMIC Core Person Vocabulary Person, Identifier, ContactPoint, Jurisdiction and Location. Do not import fictional-person semantics from FOAF or schema.org that CPV explicitly excludes. Treat CPV Address as a reusable value shape or pointer, not as this model's location master. Treat CPV sex as a boundary: store a civil marker here, not an organism trait.
Align the terms identity, attribute, identifier, principal and identity-proofing. Do not adopt ISO/IEC 24760 non-human principals into this natural-person model.

Reuse OASIS xNL structured name value shapes and customisable name-element semantics rather than inventing a new name grammar. Address value shapes may be reused from xAL by reference to a location sibling.

Use schema.org Person only as a public-projection typing. Conflict: schema.org Person includes fictional and undead characters, US-centric first/last name comments, and family properties (child, parent, sibling, spouse) that belong in a household sibling model.

Align the eIDAS minimum data set and EUDI PID mandatory attributes (current family name, current given names, date of birth, person identifier) and selective disclosure. Do not assume the person identifier is a national personal number.
Align identity-document evidence fields and MRZ/eMRTD data groups with ICAO Doc 9303. The travel document evidences the person; it is not the civil identity.

Household membership, filiation, parent, child and spouse-as-relationship live in the household or family sibling model and point to this person identifier. Civil status as a legal state remains here.
Group and community membership resolves against the person identifier and is not stored as an identity core attribute.
Earned credentials anchor to the person as holder; they are not personal-sphere self-declarations.
Civil registrars, identification authorities, document issuers, statistics offices and organisation-guardians are organisations. Employment and membership roles are out of scope.
Place of birth, place of death, domicile address and residency jurisdiction are pointers into location, address or jurisdiction masters.
Standing grants over personal-sphere and identity attributes are governed in the consent service; this model stores only pointers and lawful-basis codes.
Runtime authorisation to read or update person facts is evaluated in the access service using owner, purpose, projection and exception.
Every access, correction, verification and extract leaves an audit trail in the audit service.

owner_package_requirements: The adopting Dimension must name the civil registrar or legally recognised identification authority that owns registered identity, documents and civil status in its jurisdiction.
The adopting Dimension must expose the personal sphere to the natural person as owner, including self-view, contact points, self-declarations and consent grants.
The adopting Dimension must bind consent, access and audit to the referenced services rather than storing consent ledgers or audit stores inside the person record.
The adopting Dimension must declare which identifier schemes and which civil-status, capacity and name-part code lists apply, because no single global list is claimed.
dimension.namespace_guidance: Publish person identity under a governed namespace in priority order: the authority master identifier, then a governed IRI, then a Dimension-assigned UUID or ULID. Scheme-qualified identifiers keep their own issuing scheme IRI and issuing authority and are never rebased into the Dimension namespace; a date is never used as an identifier.

canonicalization_rules: Time values are canonicalised to RFC 3339 with seconds and an explicit offset or Z; incomplete civil dates keep GenericDate precision (full date, year-month or year) rather than being padded.
Event time is stored separately from observation and ingestion time and is never collapsed into one timestamp.

Names are canonicalised as versioned structured name records with parts, script, language tag, ordering convention and validity; the ICAO Latin transliteration is stored alongside, not instead of, the legal name.
Identifiers are canonicalised as scheme-qualified assignments carrying scheme IRI, notation, issuing authority and validity.
Country codes are canonicalised together with their code system, because EU Publications Office EL and UK differ from ISO 3166-1 GR and GB.
patch_rules: Registrar-owned facts are patched only by the registrar, through versioned corrections that record prior value, new value, legal basis, authority and correction time.
Name, marker and civil-status changes are applied as new effective-dated versions derived from registered events, never as in-place edits.
Self-declared attributes patch only the personal sphere and never overwrite legal name, civil marker or civil status.
Document revocation and identifier retirement patch the state of the attachment, not the person identity itself.
Death registration retires legal identity and does not delete the permanent register entry.
compatibility_rules: Alignments to CPV, ISO/IEC 24760, OASIS CIQ, eIDAS PID, ICAO Doc 9303 and schema.org are vocabulary alignments; incompatible semantics such as fictional persons, non-human principals and biological sex as an organism trait are not imported.
Consumers must not assume an eIDAS person identifier equals a national personal number and must not reuse pairwise identifiers as matching keys.
Name-part consumers must read the declared name-part scheme rather than assuming Anglo-American first/middle/last semantics.

identity_priority: Authoritative master-system identifier assigned by the civil registration or legally recognised identification authority
Governed global IRI published under the owning namespace
UUID or ULID assigned by the adopting Dimension when no master identifier exists
A date is never used as an identifier
artifact_rules.timestamp_rule: All artefact and record times use RFC 3339 with seconds and an explicit offset or Z; incomplete civil dates use GenericDate precision, and event time is recorded separately from observation and ingestion time.
artifact_rules.serial_naming_rule: Serially issued artefacts such as certificates, identity documents, PID credentials and protection instruments are named by the issuer-assigned number qualified by issuing authority, scheme and document type; that number identifies the artefact instance, not the person. Records, decisions, declarations, results and extracts are named by their record identifier plus owning party and time.
artifact_rules.integrity_rule: The person is the stable natural-person subject. Names, documents and identifiers attach to the person and never become the person. Registrar-owned civil facts (identity core, vital events, civil status, recorded markers, issued documents) are created only by a civil registrar or legally recognised identification authority. Person-owned personal-sphere facts are created only by the person or an authorised representative. Death retires legal identity and does not delete the permanent register. Event time and observation or ingestion time are stored separately. Verification discloses only requested attributes.

policies: Split stewardship: the civil registrar or identification authority owns registered identity, documents and civil status; the natural person owns personal-sphere data and consent over it.
ISO/IEC 24760 alignment is vocabulary-only; non-human principals cannot be stored as Person.
GDPR data minimisation, purpose limitation, accuracy, storage limitation and integrity apply to processing of person data, with the public-interest archiving exception for permanent civil registers.
Identity verification and PID presentation use selective disclosure or confirmation-only answers.
No silent overwrite of legal name, civil marker or civil status by self-declared attributes.
Special-category data, including biometrics used to uniquely identify a person, require an Article 9 condition in addition to an Article 6 basis.
Household, filiation and organisational roles must be referenced, not duplicated.
Time values use RFC 3339 with seconds and an explicit offset or Z; incomplete civil dates use GenericDate precision.

read: A relying party may read only the projection authorised for a stated purpose, typically a verification view or a legally public extract.
The person, or an authorised representative, may read the self-view of records and grants.
The civil registrar may read registrar-owned facts in its jurisdiction.
Statistical users may read only anonymised vital-statistics extracts.
create: Birth registration or legally linked identification-authority conferral creates the person record.
Only the registrar or issuing authority may create identity documents, identifier assignments and civil-status events.
Only the person or authorised representative may create personal-sphere contact points, self-declarations and consent grants.
Representation arrangements are created by the competent court, statute, or the person where the law allows.
update: Registrar-owned facts are corrected by the registrar with versioned provenance; they are not silently edited.
Name, marker and civil-status changes take effect only through registered events.
The person updates personal-sphere attributes and withdraws consent.
Document revocation and identifier retirement are updates to those attachments, not to the person identity itself.
delete: Vital-event and legal-identity register entries are not deleted; death retires identity.
Personal-sphere attributes may be erased or restricted on a valid data-subject request unless a legal-obligation or archive override applies.
Revoked documents remain historically recorded with a revoked state.
Audit records of access are retained according to the audit service, not according to personal-sphere erasure.

roles.name: Civil registrar
responsibilities: Confer and maintain legal identity through vital registration
Record legal name, birth and death facts, civil status and legally recorded markers
Issue and preserve certificates
Authorise corrections to registrar-owned facts

roles.name: Identification authority
responsibilities: Confer legal identity when birth was not registered, linked to civil registration
Issue national identity credentials where distinct from the registrar
Assign scheme-qualified national identifiers

roles.name: Natural person
responsibilities: Own personal-sphere data and consent grants
Exercise access, rectification, erasure, restriction and portability rights
Declare contact points and non-legal names
Present identity documents or PID under their control

roles.name: Document issuer
responsibilities: Issue, suspend and revoke travel documents, identity cards or digital PID
Bind the document to the person with ICAO or eIDAS mandatory fields
Maintain document validity state

roles.name: Representative or supporter
responsibilities: Support or, where national law still allows, represent the person within recorded scope
Respect will and preferences and declared conflicts of interest
Submit to review by the competent authority

roles.name: Relying party
responsibilities: Request only needed attributes at an appropriate assurance level
Accept confirmation-only or selectively disclosed answers
Not persist pairwise identifiers as national personal numbers

roles.name: Statistics office
responsibilities: Receive anonymised vital-statistics extracts
Not re-identify persons from aggregates

access.default_rule: Deny all person-data access unless the requester is the owning registrar for registrar-owned facts, the person or authorised representative for self-view and personal-sphere facts, or a relying party with a lawful basis and an authorised projection.
exceptions: Parental responsibility or recorded representation for a child or supported person, limited to the arrangement scope and review period
Court order or other legal obligation with expiry and audit identifier
Emergency vital-interests processing under GDPR Article 6(1)(d)
Legally public civil-status extracts that exclude the personal sphere
audit_requirements: Record requester, purpose, projection type, attribute identifiers disclosed or withheld, lawful basis or exception, and decision time as RFC 3339
Record corrections with prior value, new value, authority and evidence
Record consent withdrawal and erasure decisions including permanent-register overrides
Bind audit entries to the audit service rather than embedding an audit store in the person record

coverage.claim: This result is a defensible civil-identity and life-course model of a natural person grounded in UN legal identity and CRVS, SEMIC Core Person Vocabulary, ICAO travel-document evidence, OASIS name semantics, eIDAS person identification data, GDPR data-subject rights and CRPD legal-capacity text. It is not a biological, household, organisational-role or fictional-person model, and it does not claim a single global civil-status, capacity or name-part code list.

checklist.notes: Canonical master identifier, governed IRI, Dimension UUID/ULID fallback; identifiers and documents are attachments; dates are not identifiers.
Birth conferral, late or identification-authority conferral, document issue and revocation, name and status changes, death retirement; presumed-death restoration marked as a national-law gap.
Citizenship, representation, document issuer and identifier authority are in scope; household, filiation, spouse-as-relationship and group membership are referenced out.
RFC 3339 event versus observation time; GenericDate for incomplete civil dates; validity periods on names, identifiers, documents, status, capacity and contact.
Asserter, evidence artefact, event time and ingestion time on facts; versioned corrections.
Registrar owns civil identity facts; person owns personal sphere and consent; split stewardship is an integrity rule.
Scheme-qualified identifiers, ICAO MRZ fields, eIDAS MDS, name-part vocabularies, duplicate detection and completeness of UN legal-identity characteristics.
Projection-based default deny, selective disclosure, representation exceptions and audit of every disclosure.
UN permanent civil register versus GDPR erasure; death retires identity; personal-sphere erasure remains possible where no archive override applies.
Alignments to CPV, ISO/IEC 24760, OASIS CIQ, eIDAS PID, ICAO 9303 and schema.org Person, with explicit conflicts recorded.
CRPD Article 12 support model plus remaining national substitute decision-making and GDPR child consent; conflict not resolved.
Place of birth and death, domicile pointer and residency jurisdiction; address master excluded.
Certificates as legal instruments, document revocation, incomplete dates, late registration and CIQ data-quality stance on unstructured names.

known_omissions: No extracted primary UN paragraph was located in this pass for foundlings, confidential birth (including accouchement sous X), intersex markers, or identity restoration after presumed death; those are recorded as likely operating cases, not as canonical UN rules.
ISO/IEC 24760-1 normative text is paywalled; terms used here are those confirmed by the ISO abstract/OBP statement and the IDPro review.
Religious personal-status systems and indigenous naming authorities beyond CIQ extensibility are not specified.
Population-register (Nordic-style) versus event-register architectures are acknowledged by UN LIA interoperability language but not modelled as alternative masters.
Posthumous personality, digital remains, nasciturus/unborn legal subjectivity, and biometric matching thresholds lack primary support in the sources used.
World Bank ID4D, NIST SP 800-63 and W3C DID/VC were not fetched within the source budget; they are likely omissions for digital-identity assurance and self-sovereign identifiers.
Hague conventions on protection of adults and apostille legalisation of civil documents were not fetched.
conflicts: CPV Person excludes imaginary people; schema.org Person includes fictional and undead characters.
CPV 2.1.2 sex is defined as the organism's biological sex, which this civil-identity model must not own; UN LIA lists sex as a legal-identity characteristic; ICAO uses M/F/X.
CPV domicile (Address: permanent home) and residency (Jurisdiction: dwelling) have overlapping usage notes versus classical domicile/habitual-residence law.
CPV citizenship versus ICAO nationality are not the same legal concept.
EU Publications Office country codes EL and UK versus ISO 3166-1 GR and GB.
CRPD Article 12 and Committee General Comment No. 1 require supported rather than substitute decision-making; most national guardianship laws still substitute.
GDPR erasure and storage limitation versus UN civil registration as continuous and permanent; GDPR generally concerns living natural persons, while death-retired records persist.
eIDAS unique identifiers may be pairwise or derived and must not be treated as national personal numbers.
ISO/IEC 24760 applies to non-human principals; this model does not.
Anglo-American first/middle/last name semantics (default CIQ samples, schema.org comments, eIDAS given/family split) versus cultures without those parts.
regional_assumptions: UN CRVSID is treated as the global operating frame: civil registration as identity factory, identity management as credentialing, vital statistics as reuse. Common-law splits between vital records and identity cards, and Nordic population registers, must be mapped into that frame rather than assumed identical.
Age of majority is jurisdiction-specific; GDPR Article 8 child-consent ages vary by Member State.
Latin MRZ transliteration is mandatory for ICAO documents even when the legal name is in another script.
EU eIDAS PID and CPV are authoritative inside the Union and alignments elsewhere, not world law.
Refugee identity may be issued by UNHCR or another mandated authority only where the host State so recognises.
adversarial_checks: Could a legal person, device, fictional character or FHIR Patient be stored as this Person? Rejected by CPV non-imaginary natural-person rule, GDPR natural-person definition, and explicit organism/health exclusion.
Could a passport number or eIDAS UID be treated as the person? Rejected by ISO/IEC 24760 identifier-versus-identity distinction and eIDAS pairwise-identifier matching rules.
Could household membership or parent/child links be copied into this model from schema.org? Rejected; those properties are sibling-model references only.
Could self-declared gender overwrite the civil marker or ICAO document field without a civil event? Rejected by split ownership and marker-change as a registered event.
Could death or an erasure request destroy the civil register? Rejected: death retires identity; the register is permanent; erasure applies to personal-sphere data unless law archives it.
Could substitute guardianship be modelled as if CRPD had abolished it worldwide? Rejected: Article 12 text plus the documented Committee-versus-State conflict must both be representable.
